Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the AeroDef Technologies Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Jenkins, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroDef Technologies' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are John Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; David Kowalski, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer; and Tom Ellis, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Actual results could differ materially due to various risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of these risks.

John Harlan:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. AeroDef Technologies delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, commercial aerospace, and space. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. With a record $145 billion backlog and a book-to-bill ratio of 1.3x, we have exceptional visibility into future growth.

As we wrap up a transformative Q3, let me turn to our strategic priorities and outlook for Q4 and FY25. We're laser-focused on executing against our core pillars: accelerating defense modernization programs, scaling our commercial aerospace recovery, expanding in high-growth space and hypersonics, and fortifying supply chain resilience amid geopolitical volatility. These priorities are underpinned by our massive backlog, up 18% year-over-year, providing multi-year revenue streams.

Let me break this down by segment, with specific guidance and insights.

First, Defense Systems—our largest contributor at 55% of revenue. We're prioritizing next-generation air dominance and missile defense, capitalizing on the U.S. DoD's FY25 budget request of $849.8 billion, which includes $28 billion for hypersonics and $18 billion for NGAD. Our HAWC-derived glide vehicle program, now in low-rate initial production Phase 2, secured $2.4 billion in new bookings this quarter from the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office. We expect this to ramp to full-rate production by mid-2025, driving 15% segment growth in FY25.

Regionally, Indo-Pacific tensions are a tailwind: We've seen a 25% uptick in orders from allies like Japan and Australia under AUKUS Pillar II, including integration of our next-gen AESA radars on F-35 platforms. In Europe, NATO's 2% GDP spending pledge, now exceeded by 23 members, has boosted our Patriot GEM-T interceptor sales by 30% year-over-year, with deliveries accelerating to Poland and Romania amid Ukraine sustainment needs. For Q4, Defense revenue guidance is $4.7 billion, up 14% year-over-year, with segment adjusted operating margins expanding 150 basis points to 13.5% on production efficiencies and fixed-price contract wins.

Second, Commercial Aerospace, at 25% of mix. Post-pandemic recovery remains robust, with global passenger traffic now at 98% of 2019 levels per IATA data. Our widebody programs, including composites for Boeing 787 derivatives and nacelles for the 777X, are fully ramping. We've invested $250 million in IR&D for hybrid-electric propulsion systems, targeting 20% fuel burn reduction by 2027—aligned with FAA sustainability goals and Airbus ZEROe concepts. Supply chain headwinds persist, with titanium pricing up 12% due to Ukraine disruptions, but our dual-sourcing from U.S. and India mitigated impacts to under 2% cost variance.

Q4 outlook: $2.1 billion in revenue, plus 22% year-over-year, fueled by 737 MAX aftermarket MRO contracts. FY25 guidance: $9.5 billion total, 16% growth, margins at 11-12% as we hit 85% capacity utilization.

Third, Space & Advanced Technologies, growing fastest at 20% of revenue. This is our innovation engine. Our smallsat constellation for SDA Tranche 2—delivering proliferated LEO comms with optical inter-satellite links—booked $1.8 billion this quarter, outpacing recent competitor wins. We're also advancing directed energy weapons, with our 300kW solid-state laser demonstrator passing Army HEL trials, positioning us for $500 million in FY25 follow-ons.

Geopolitically, China's ASAT tests and Russia's space-based threats underscore urgency; U.S. Space Force funding rose 7% to $30 billion in FY25. Internationally, ESA partnerships for Ariane 6 upper stages add €400 million in backlog. Q4 Space revenue: $1.6 billion, up 28% year-over-year; FY25: $7.2 billion, 25% growth, margins 14-15% on scale.

Cross-cutting priorities include digital transformation and resilience. We're deploying AI/ML for predictive maintenance across programs—reducing F-35 sustainment costs by 18% in simulations—and allocating $400 million to domestic supply chains via the Defense Production Act, targeting criticals like rare earths and GaN semiconductors. ESG-wise, 35% of our energy now from renewables, with SAF trials on our test fleet.

Full-year outlook and Q4 guidance: For FY24, we're raising revenue to $72.5 billion from $72.0 billion previously, EPS to $10.50 from $10.20, and free cash flow to $4.8 billion. Q4: Revenue $18.4 billion, up 16% year-over-year, EPS $2.75, book-to-bill 1.2x. FY25 full-year: Revenue $80 billion, up 11%, EPS $11.50-$12.00, FCF $5.2 billion, assuming no major disruptions.

In summary, with global defense spending projected at $2.44 trillion per SIPRI 2024 estimates, up 6.8% in real terms, escalating great-power competition, and commercial aviation's structural rebound, AeroDef is uniquely positioned. Our $12 billion in FY25 IRAD/capex underscores commitment to tech leadership. We're confident in delivering superior shareholder returns while safeguarding national security.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our HAWC-derived hypersonic program and its potential to accelerate our defense segment growth. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily.

David Kowalski:
Thank you, John. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $18.7 billion, representing a 14% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $2.62. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $4.5 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year has been raised as John noted. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 15.8%, operating income of $2.27 billion, and free cash flow of $1.2 billion.

Good morning, everyone. As we wrap up a quarter where we delivered record free cash flow of $1.2 billion—up 25% year-over-year on the back of our $145 billion backlog and a book-to-bill ratio of 1.3x—it's a perfect time to dive into our capital deployment strategy. In the Aerospace & Defense sector, where program lifecycles span decades and geopolitical tailwinds like the US FY24 NDAA's $886 billion topline are driving sustained demand, we've maintained a disciplined, multi-pronged approach. This balances immediate shareholder returns via dividends and buybacks with long-term growth through tuck-in acquisitions and organic reinvestment.

First, dividends. Our shareholders have been the clear beneficiaries of our consistent cash generation. We've now increased our quarterly dividend for the 12th straight year, raising it 8% to $0.65 per share, payable December 15th to shareholders of record by November 30th. This brings our full-year payout to $2.52 per share, yielding approximately 1.8% at current prices—right in line with sector peers like Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, but with a payout ratio of just 35% of adjusted net income, leaving ample room for growth. This reflects our confidence in enduring revenue streams from fixed-price development contracts on programs like the F-35 Lightning II sustainment—where we're booking $2.5 billion annually—and the ramp in hypersonic weapons under the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon initiative.

Moving to share repurchases. We've been aggressive here, executing $1.8 billion under our $3 billion authorization announced last February. That's $1.2 billion repurchased in the first nine months alone, at an average price of $185 per share, retiring about 2.1% of our outstanding float. This has accreted roughly $0.45 to adjusted EPS this year, and with our ROIC north of 18%—bolstered by PTTR metrics exceeding 70% on legacy programs—we see buybacks as a high-ROI use of capital, especially when our stock trades at 18x forward EBITDA, a discount to RTX's 20x multiple amid commercial aero recovery headwinds. We've paused new authorizations for now to prioritize M&A, but with $4.5 billion in cash on hand and net debt at a healthy 1.8x EBITDA, we'll opportunistically deploy more in 2025 if valuations remain attractive.

Acquisitions remain a cornerstone, targeting adjacencies in high-growth vectors like unmanned systems, C4ISR, and space resilience—areas where DoD spending is surging 12% year-over-year per the Congressional Budget Office. Year-to-date, we closed two deals totaling $850 million: the $450 million acquisition of SkyNet Dynamics, a leader in AI-enabled Group 3 UAS with ISR payloads integrating seamlessly into our MQ-Next portfolio, and the $400 million buy of QuantumShield Cyber, enhancing our zero-trust architectures for JADC2 networks. These are immediately accretive, adding 150 basis points to margins through cost synergies and cross-selling into our $12 billion services backlog. Looking ahead, our M&A pipeline exceeds $2 billion, with a focus on Indo-Pacific capabilities—think counter-drone tech for AUKUS partners—and European expansion amid the €100 billion German Zeus special fund and Ukraine aid replenishments. We're disciplined on pricing, targeting 8-10x EBITDA multiples, avoiding the froth we saw in 2021 SPAC deals.

Regionally, this strategy plays to our strengths: 65% US-centric revenue shields us from FX volatility, while exports—up 15% to $4.2 billion—capitalize on NATO's 2% GDP pledges and Gulf sovereign demand for THAAD interceptors. Supply chain normalization, with titanium costs down 20% from 2022 peaks, has unlocked $300 million in working capital, fueling this deployment.

Strategically, we're threading the needle between returns and innovation. Capex is targeted at $1.1 billion for 2024, focused on digital thread initiatives at our Fort Worth NGAD skunkworks and additive manufacturing for Vulcan-class rocket boosters amid the Space Force's $30 billion FY25 ask. Debt reduction—$500 million year-to-date—keeps our investment-grade profile intact, with all-in yields under 4%. Peering RTX and LMT, our total shareholder yield of 4.5% (dividends + buybacks + debt paydown) outperforms the sector average, underscoring our commitment to capital efficiency in a world of rising threats from hypersonic glide vehicles to contested LEO orbits.

Today, I'll dive deep into our gross margin, operating margin, and net income performance for Q3, providing the color on the key drivers, segment dynamics, and forward-looking insights that position us strongly in this dynamic Aerospace & Defense landscape. Our results reflect the resilience of our portfolio—spanning legacy platforms like the F-35 Lightning II joint strike fighter program, where we're a key Tier 1 supplier, to next-gen hypersonics and space systems amid escalating geopolitical tensions from Ukraine to the Indo-Pacific.

Gross margins came in at 15.8% for the quarter, up 160 basis points year-over-year from 14.2% and marking our strongest Q3 gross margin in five years. On a trailing twelve-month basis, we're now at 15.4%, trending toward our long-term target of 16-17% by FY2026. This expansion was driven by a pristine mix shift across our Defense and Space segments, which accounted for 72% of Q3 revenue—up from 68% last year—bolstered by high-margin fixed-price development contracts on programs like the Next Generation Air Dominance demonstrator and our ARRW hypersonic weapon system.

Key tailwinds included supply chain de-risking: we realized $120 million in year-to-date cost savings through our Enterprise Digital Supply Chain initiative, leveraging AI-driven predictive analytics and additive manufacturing for titanium components on the F-35 center fuselage. This reduced scrap rates by 22% and shaved 15% off raw material variances. Pricing discipline on aftermarket spares—up 8% on commercial aero engines like our CFM56 equivalents—also contributed 40 basis points of expansion. Offsetting some pressure was commercial aviation recovery, where Boeing 737 MAX supply chain snarls from Spirit AeroSystems’ quality issues lingered, compressing segment margins to 11.2% from 10.8%. Regionally, U.S. DoD awards surged 12% to $4.2 billion, fueled by the FY2024 NDAA supplemental for Pacific deterrence, while European F-35 ramp-ups added $450 million at 18% margins. Asia-Pacific, however, saw a 5% dip due to delayed Indian MRFA contract awards amid Rafale competition.

Operating margins delivered 12.1% for the quarter—expanding 90 basis points from 11.2% last year and up 70 basis points sequentially. Trailing twelve months now at 11.8%, this reflects disciplined OpEx management amid inflationary headwinds. Adjusted operating income rose 14% to $2.27 billion on $18.7 billion of revenue, with SG&A flat at 4.2% of sales despite $25 million in one-time cyber resilience investments post the CMMC 2.0 compliance push.

R&D spend held steady at 5.1% of revenue—$955 million—including $180 million funneled into digital engineering twins for our GhostWorks autonomous drone swarm tech. This not only amortized favorably but unlocked $60 million in cost avoids on sustainment contracts. Labor efficiencies from our ‘Skills Forward’ upskilling program—certifying 2,500 engineers in Model-Based Systems Engineering—cut indirect rates by 10%. Headwinds? A 300 basis point wage inflation hit in our Fort Worth facility, partially mitigated by offshoring 15% of machining to low-cost Mexico sites under USMCA. Segmentally, Defense op margins hit 14.3% (up from 13.1%), Space at 13.7% (led by GPS IIIF satellite production), while Commercial held at 7.9% amid Pratt & Whitney GTF engine recall costs rippling through the supply base.

Net income attributable to AeroDef shareholders was $1.53 billion, or $2.62 diluted EPS—up 17% and 16% year-over-year, respectively, beating our guidance midpoint. This translates to a 8.2% net margin, our best Q3 since the JASSM lot pricing settlements in 2019. The $120 million beat to consensus stemmed from lower-than-expected interest expense—down 8% to $85 million—thanks to our $2.5 billion debt refinancing at 4.1% fixed rates in Q1, and a 24.5% effective tax rate aided by R&D credits on classified hypersonics work.

Non-operating items were clean: no new legacy pension charges, and FX headwinds from a stronger USD shaved just $10 million off international sales (primarily Australia’s Loyal Wingman program). Free cash flow supported a $450 million share repurchase, reducing shares outstanding by 1.2%.

Strategically, these metrics underscore our pivot to high-margin sustainment and tech infusion. With the DoD’s Replicator initiative prioritizing 1,000+ attritable drones by 2026, we’re targeting 200 basis points of gross margin accretion from autonomy scale-up. Risks remain—supply chain fragility from U.S. steel tariffs and China’s rare earth dominance—but our $145 billion backlog, 40% at >15% margins, and 1.4x book-to-bill provide a fortress balance sheet. Looking to Q4, we guide gross margins to 16.0-16.3%, op margins to 12.3-12.6%, and EPS to $2.75-$2.85, positioning FY2024 for mid-teens net income growth.

Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our analysis of revenue drivers and headwinds for the quarter, providing some color on what fueled our top-line growth and the challenges we're navigating.

Q3 revenue came in at $18.7 billion, up 14% year-over-year and 8% sequentially, driven primarily by our Defense Systems segment, which accounted for 58% of total revenue—up from 52% last year. This marks the third straight quarter of double-digit growth, supported by a record $145 billion backlog, with 65% funded and visibility extending into FY27.

Primary revenue drivers: First, Defense Programs. This segment delivered $10.9 billion, a robust 22% year-over-year increase, fueled by accelerated deliveries on our hypersonic weapons suite and next-gen ISR platforms. Notably, the Lot 15 low-rate initial production contract for the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter—valued at $4.2 billion—ramped ahead of schedule, with 28 aircraft handed over to the USAF and international partners like the UK and Israel. We're also seeing strong pull from missile defense, where our SM-6 Block IB interceptor saw a 35% volume uptick, driven by U.S. Navy Multi-Year Procurement awards totaling $2.8 billion. Geopolitically, heightened tensions in the Indo-Pacific have boosted demand for our Pacific Deterrence Initiative packages, including the LRASM, with export orders from Japan and Australia adding $1.1 billion to the quarter.

Second, Commercial Aviation. Representing 32% of revenue at $6.0 billion—up 9% year-over-year—we're benefiting from the post-pandemic travel rebound. Narrow-body aftermarket services for the Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo families grew 18%, as airlines like Delta and Southwest ramped MRO activity amid high utilization rates. Our wide-body OEM business, including composite structures for the 787 Dreamliner and A350 XWB, contributed $2.4 billion, supported by Boeing's production stabilization at 38 per month and Airbus targeting 75 A320s monthly by year-end. A key tailwind here is our digital thread initiative, leveraging Siemens NX and digital twins to reduce lead times by 25%, which helped us capture 15% market share in SAF-compatible nacelles.

Third, Space and Emerging Tech. This high-margin segment hit $1.8 billion, up 25% year-over-year, with standout performance from our satellite constellations for NRO tasking and commercial LEO broadband. Partnerships with SpaceX on Starship upper-stage components and Blue Origin's New Glenn have diversified our revenue, now 12% from non-U.S. government sources.

Regionally, North America remains our bedrock at 72% of revenue, but international exposure grew to 28%, led by Middle East sustainment contracts (up 30% year-over-year) for F-15EX platforms with Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and APAC growth from AUKUS-related submarine propulsion tech.

Key headwinds and mitigations: Supply chain disruptions shaved 3 points off our organic growth, particularly Pratt & Whitney's GTF engine durability issues, which delayed 737 MAX deliveries by 45 days and inflated working capital by $450 million. Raw material inflation—titania and carbon fiber up 12%—coupled with skilled labor shortages in our Oklahoma and Alabama facilities, drove segment COGS up 7% to 68% of sales.

Programmatic headwinds include FAA certification delays on our Hybrid-Electric Propulsion demonstrator, pushing $300 million of revenue into Q1 FY25, and Boeing's ongoing 737 MAX quality scrutiny, which tempered aftermarket volumes. Geopolitically, U.S. export controls under ITAR have slowed $200 million in hypersonic tech transfers to allies, though we're offsetting this via licensed production in the UK.

On a macro level, foreign exchange headwinds from a stronger USD deducted 2% from reported growth, with Eurozone weakness impacting Airbus-related flows.

Looking ahead, our revenue trajectory remains strong, with FY24 guidance raised to $72.5-74.5 billion, implying 12-15% growth. We're leaning into three pillars: derisking supply chains through our $1.2 billion Vertical Integration Plan—insourcing 40% of aerostructures by 2026; tech infusion, like AI-optimized additive manufacturing for C-130J wings, targeting 20% productivity gains; and portfolio balancing, growing Space to 15% of revenue via Artemis lunar lander bids and hypersonic sustainment.

Good morning, everyone. As we wrap up a strong quarter, let me turn to our full-year 2024 guidance and provide segment-level detail on revenue and earnings expectations. Overall, we're maintaining our consolidated revenue guidance at $72.5 billion to $74.5 billion, representing 6% to 8% organic growth year-over-year, driven by robust program executions, a $145 billion backlog—up 12% sequentially—and accelerating international Foreign Military Sales. Adjusted segment operating profit is guided at $10.8 billion to $11.2 billion, with margins expanding 50 to 75 basis points to 14.9% to 15.1%, reflecting improved fixed-price contract performance, cost-out initiatives, and higher-volume sustainment revenue.

Aeronautics Segment: Raising full-year revenue guidance to $26.0 billion to $26.5 billion, up 9% to 12% from 2023, fueled by F-35 Lot 17 and Lot 18 LRIP deliveries—now expecting 156 aircraft versus our prior 148—and ramping F-16 Block 70/72 exports. Q4 should see $6.8 billion in revenue, with sequential growth from C-130J Super Hercules sustainment contracts valued at $2.5 billion annually.

Earnings-wise, segment operating profit is guided at $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion, with margins at 13.0% to 13.6%—a 150 bps expansion—thanks to $450 million in affordability improvements from our Enterprise Affordability Initiative, including digital twins for wing assembly reducing labor hours by 18%. U.S. DoD funding remains stable at $28 billion in the FY25 President's Budget request, but we're monitoring sequestration risks. Internationally, F-35 wins in Finland and Poland add $4 billion to the backlog, with Asia-Pacific tensions boosting Block 70 interest from Indonesia and Slovakia. Key initiative: Advancing NGAD digital engineering prototypes under the Air Force's $2.5 billion FY25 increment.

Missiles and Fire Control Segment: Revenue guidance is now $20.2 billion to $20.7 billion, implying 11% to 14% growth, led by PAC-3 MSE interceptors—with production scaling to 550 units annually—and JASSM-ER/JASSM-XR hypersonic variants. Q4 revenue expected at $5.4 billion, including $1.2 billion from Precision Strike Missiles for Army long-range fires modernization.

Operating profit: $4.1 billion to $4.3 billion, margins steady at 20.3% to 20.8%, supported by 85% fixed-price contract mix and supply chain resilience via our Titanium Flowdown Program, mitigating 2024's 15% raw material inflation. Trends show munition stockpiles at 18-month war reserve levels post-Ukraine drawdowns, driving a $15 billion backlog surge. Europe: $3.5 billion in FMS for NASAMS and HIMARS to NATO allies. Strategically, $250 million in directed energy weapons CRADAs with DARPA.

Rotary and Mission Systems Segment: Guidance holds at $15.8 billion to $16.3 billion in revenue, up 5% to 8%, with steady-state Black Hawk UH-60M deliveries (48 units) and MH-60R Seahawk exports to Australia. Q4 at $4.2 billion, bolstered by $800 million in mission systems upgrades.

Profit: $2.0 billion to $2.1 billion, margins 12.6% to 12.9%, with 100 bps upside from C4ISR software-defined radios under the Army's $2 billion IDIQ. Labor headwinds persist, but our $100 million apprenticeship program is yielding 15% productivity gains. Middle East FMS for Apache AH-64E strong at $2 billion. Initiative: AI/ML for autonomous rotorcraft under FVL.

Space Segment: Revenue guided at $10.5 billion to $10.8 billion, flat to 3% growth amid NASA SLS/Orion delays, offset by GPS IIIF satellite launches (three in Q4) and missile warning payloads. Q4 revenue $2.7 billion.

Operating profit: $1.3 billion to $1.4 billion, margins 12.4% to 12.9%, pressured by 20% launch cost overruns but mitigated by $300 million in commercial LEO constellations. Backlog $12 billion, with DoD Space Force at $30 billion FY25. Key trend: Proliferated LEO driving 25% annual demand growth. AUKUS adds $1 billion upside.

In summary, our guidance embeds $500 million in supply chain tailwinds from CHIPS Act funding for gallium nitride chips, but we flag $200 million to $400 million in potential FY25 headwinds from Continuing Resolution delays. Backlog conversion remains at 25% annually, with 40% international mix. We're well-positioned for FY25's $850 billion NDAA topline.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, David. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies to improve efficiency and reduce costs. Specifically, moving to updates on our key programs, which represent the core of our $28.5 billion backlog and drive over 70% of our projected FY24 revenue. I'll break this down by platform, highlighting development progress, production ramps, key milestones, and strategic implications amid supply chain headwinds and geopolitical tailwinds. Our programs remain on track to deliver low double-digit EPS growth, supported by fixed-price incentives and cost-plus sustainment tails.

Starting with our flagship Next-Generation Air Dominance program. We're in the late Engineering and Manufacturing Development phase, with our demonstrator aircraft achieving first flight in Q2—six months ahead of schedule—validating our adaptive cycle engine architecture, which delivers 25% better thrust-specific fuel consumption than legacy F135s on the F-35. Production-wise, we've transitioned to Low-Rate Initial Production Lot 1, delivering three test articles to the USAF in Q3, up from zero last year. We're ramping to 12 units in FY25, with full-rate production targeted for FY27 at 48 per year, aligning with CCAM integration. Backlog here stands at $12.4 billion, with 85% funded. We're mitigating titanium supply constraints—up 18% in pricing due to Russian sanctions—through dual-sourcing from Japan and Australia, while digital twin simulations have reduced certification risks by 30%. Export interest from the UK and Japan under GCAP could add $5-7 billion in FMS by decade-end.

Shifting to hypersonics, our Glide Phase Interceptor program for MDA's Next-Gen Interceptor is a standout. We've hit a major milestone: successful end-to-end flight test from Kauai in August, achieving Mach 7+ glide with 95% hit probability against an ICBM surrogate. Development is at TRL 8, with production contracts awarded for 20 Boost Glide Vehicles in Q3, recognizing $450 million in revenue this quarter alone, a 40% year-over-year increase. We're scaling to 50 per year by FY26, supported by a $3.2 billion backlog. Technical initiatives include our proprietary carbon-carbon composites for thermal protection, shaving 15% off weight versus incumbents. Amid U.S.-China tensions, this positions us for Pacific Deterrence Initiative funding; we've secured $800 million in INDOPACOM prototypes.

On the rotary-wing side, our Future Vertical Lift Future Long-Range Assault Aircraft remains a growth engine. Milestone C achieved in Q1, greenlighting FRP with 18 aircraft delivered year-to-date, 25% ahead of plan, ramping to 36 per year by FY25. Sustainment revenues hit $620 million in Q3, up 12% year-over-year, driven by MRO contracts with performance-based logistics yielding 98% mission capability rates. Backlog is $8.1 billion, with international pursuits in Poland and Saudi Arabia via FMS channels. Avionics delays from Honeywell pushed one delivery, but we've derisked via parallel qualification, maintaining EBITDA margins at 14.5%.

In space systems, our Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture satellite constellation for the Space Force is accelerating. We've launched Batch 2's 18 satellites via SpaceX Falcon 9 in September—on time, under budget—bringing total on-orbit to 42, with 99.7% availability for tactical SATCOM relay. Production rate is now 24 per year at our new Chandler, AZ facility, up from 12 in FY23, with Q3 bookings of $1.1 billion pushing backlog to $4.7 billion. Integration of pLEO mesh networking enables 10x latency reduction over legacy GEO birds. NRO tasking for ISR payloads supports Ukraine aid, while commercial hyperspectral imaging cross-sells diversify revenues.

Finally, our commercial aerospace exposure via the Ultra-High Bypass Turbofan engine for Boeing's 777X program. Certification slips at Boeing delayed two deliveries, but we've recognized $320 million on 14 shipped modules, with production stabilizing at eight per month. This hedges our defense skew, capturing 22% share in the LEAP-1B aftermarket amid Pratt & Whitney GTF durability issues.

Overall, program execution is robust: deliveries up 17% year-over-year across platforms, with DCUARS metrics showing 96% on-schedule performance. We're leaning into JADC2 convergence, investing $250 million in AI/ML for predictive logistics, targeting 20% margin expansion in sustainment by FY27. Geopolitically, supplemental budgets from Israel/Gaza and Ukraine sustain demand.

Dr. Raj Patel:
Thank you, Lisa. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in our next-generation propulsion systems, including adaptive cycle engines and hypersonic glide vehicles. We anticipate these advancements will give us a competitive edge in the years to come. More specifically, our directed energy lasers and AI-enabled UAS integrations are advancing rapidly, with recent trials validating performance in contested environments and positioning us ahead in NGAD and SDA programs.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Friedman with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Josh Friedman:
Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on the supply chain headwinds, particularly in commercial aero and titanium pricing?

John Harlan:
Certainly, Josh. We've navigated these effectively through dual-sourcing strategies from U.S., India, Japan, and Australia, limiting cost variances to under 2% despite 12-18% pricing increases tied to Ukraine and sanctions. Our Enterprise Digital Supply Chain initiative delivered $120 million in savings via AI predictive analytics and additive manufacturing, reducing scrap by 22%. For Q4 and FY25, our Vertical Integration Plan insources 40% of aerostructures, derisking further while CHIPS Act funding supports GaN chips.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the revenue and earnings guidance by segment—any changes there?

David Kowalski:
Maria, great question. As detailed, Aeronautics raised to $26-26.5 billion revenue, Missiles $20.2-20.7 billion, Rotary $15.8-16.3 billion, Space $10.5-10.8 billion, with margins expanding across the board on fixed-price ramps and affordability gains. FY25 embeds strong growth from hypersonics and LEO, assuming stable DoD budgets.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Peter Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Peter Kim:
Thanks. Regarding the updates on key programs like NGAD and hypersonics—what are the latest milestones?

Dr. Raj Patel:
Peter, happy to elaborate. NGAD demonstrator first flight six months early, now in LRIP Lot 1 with three deliveries; hypersonics GPI hit Mach 7+ in August Kauai test at 95% accuracy, scaling to 50/year by FY26. FVL FLRAA at Milestone C, 18 delivered ahead of plan; PWSA Batch 2 launched on-time. All on track with 96% schedule performance.

John Harlan:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. A replay will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
